title: Trellis Connector: async kernel tiling experiments and KV-prefetch tradeoffs
content:
Summary:

This note captures a series of exploratory experiments for a lightweight integration layer we are calling the "Trellis Connector" — a thin async bridge that permits live routing between Triton-managed model instances, TensorRT-optimized kernels, and a tiny custom kernel shim. The goal is to evaluate tiling strategies, priority-driven scheduling, and KV-cache prefetch/eviction tradeoffs when mixing heterogeneous runtimes on a single GPU.

Why this matters:
- Customers run mixed workloads (streaming chat + rerank + embeddings) and we need to keep tail latency low while maximizing GPU utilization.
- Full process-level fallbacks (cold switching from Triton to TRT engine) can add 20–150ms tail latency; an in-GPU connector that can switch call-paths at op granularity can reduce that significantly if memory and kernel coherence are managed.

Hypothesis:
1) An async bridge that tiles long sequences into prioritized micro-batches and routes subgraphs to the most cost-effective kernel (TRT, Triton CPU fallback, custom op) will improve P50 and P95 latency for mixed workloads while increasing aggregate tokens/s.
2) Aggressive KV-prefetch (prefix-aware) pays off for long-context chat patterns but harms throughput for very short requests due to memory pressure and kernel eviction churn.

Testbed and configuration:
- Hardware: 1x NVIDIA H100-80GB, 1x NVIDIA A100-40GB (for cross-run comparisons)
- Software: Triton 23.10, TensorRT 9.5, CUDA 12.2, cuDNN 9.5, custom-shim v0.3 (in-process kernel loader)
- Models: llama-like 7B (fp16), opt-6.7b (quantized int8 profile), a minimal reranker MLP (custom kernel)
- Workloads: (A) streaming chat (median tokens 120, P99 tokens 1024), (B) batch rerank (N=64), (C) embeddings (N=128 short sequences) in mixed ratios 60/25/15
- Metrics: P50/P95/P99 latency (ms), throughput tokens/s, GPU memory used (MB), kernel warmup latency (ms), number of kernel swaps per minute, kv-cache hit ratio

Key primitives tested:
- async-tiling: break long sequences into tiles (tile sizes 64/128/256) and schedule via priority queue (higher priority = streaming tail tokens)
- kernel-affinity: a heuristic that prefers TRT for dense attention, custom-shim for small MLPs, Triton for unknown ops or safety fallback
- kv-prefetch: prefix-aware prefetch of KV slices into a dedicated slab cache; eviction policy either LRU or prefix-weighted LRU (weights proportional to recent access frequency)
- hot-swap: in-GPU kernel switch that avoids process restart by keeping both kernels resident and switching dispatch pointer; fallback cold-swap tears down and reloads engine

Experiment matrix (representative runs):
1) Baseline: Triton-only serving with standard KV cache (LRU), no tiling.
2) Trellis-tiling + default affinity, LRU kv-cache.
3) Trellis-tiling + affinity + prefix-weighted kv-prefetch (cache cap 18GB on H100).
4) Trellis + minimal custom-shim for reranker + hot-swap enabled (both TRT and shim resident).
5) Aggressive tiling (tile=64) + frequent eviction (cache cap 12GB) to stress eviction churn.

Representative results (H100, mixed workload 60/25/15):
- Baseline (Triton-only): P50=18ms, P95=138ms, P99=310ms, tokens/s=46k, GPU mem=54GB, kv-hit=0.61
- Trellis (tile=128, affinity): P50=16ms, P95=94ms, P99=185ms, tokens/s=62k, GPU mem=60GB, kv-hit=0.58, kernel-swaps/min=6
- Trellis + prefix-prefetch (cap=18GB): P50=15ms, P95=82ms, P99=142ms, tokens/s=68k, GPU mem=68GB, kv-hit=0.82, kernel-swaps/min=8
- Trellis + hot-swap resident kernels: P50=15ms, P95=76ms, P99=120ms, tokens/s=71k, GPU mem=69GB, kv-hit=0.79, kernel-swaps/min=2, hot-swap-latency approx 4.5ms
- Aggressive tiling + low cap: P50=14ms, P95=210ms, P99=520ms, tokens/s=53k, GPU mem=64GB, kv-hit=0.44, kernel-swaps/min=24

Interpretation:
- Tiling with affinity routing improves throughput and P95 significantly versus baseline by allowing higher kernel specialization and better packing.
- Prefix-aware kv-prefetch raises hit ratio and throughput but increases resident memory. It reduces P99 substantially for long-context streaming because it serves KV from the slab instead of re-computing or thrashing between kernels.
- Hot-swap (resident kernels) is the most effective at preventing cold-engine penalties. The measured hot-swap dispatch pointer change was ~4–6ms; the major overhead remains memory duplication when both engine variants co-reside.
- Aggressive tiling with small cache caps causes eviction churn; the per-eviction overhead (kernel reloads and KV migrations) spikes P95/P99, undoing gains from finer-grained tiling.

Tradeoffs and operational considerations:
1) Memory vs. latency: maintaining multiple resident kernels + a large kv slab increases GPU memory pressure and may force per-tenant capacity fragmentation. For Dedicated customers that want predictable SLOs, we should expose an explicit policy: resident-kernels: {none, essential-only, all-compatible} and kv-cache-cap (GB).
2) Cost complexity: prefix-prefetch improves quality for chat-heavy customers but has a cost (reserved memory). We can surface an optimization recommendation in Console (e.g., enable prefix-prefetch when median seq length > 128 and >40% of requests are streaming).
3) Scheduler fairness: priority tiling benefits streaming tails but can starve bulk jobs (rerank). Implement token-level fairness windows and preemption points so rerank batches are guaranteed progress over time-slices.
4) Observability: need fine metrics: per-kernel residency, swaps/min, per-tenant kv-hit by prefix-length, tile-induced latency distributions. Add trace spans around tile boundary dispatching and KV migration.

API/Config sketch (proposal):
- trellis.connector.enabled: bool
- trellis.connector.tile_size: int (64|128|256) / auto
- trellis.connector.affinity_policy: [cost_optimized | latency_optimized | balanced]
- trellis.connector.kv.prefetch: [off | prefix-weighted | eager]
- trellis.connector.kv.cap_gb: int
- trellis.connector.kernel_residency: [none | essential-only | full]
- trellis.connector.fairness_window_ms: int (default 200)

Open questions / next experiments:
- Multi-GPU: how does Trellis behave when kernels are sharded across devices (KV coherence across NVLink)? We need a follow-up test with 4x A100 split workloads.
- Quantization interplay: TRT int8 engines reduced memory but changed hot-swap behavior (engine compatibility issue). Test sequence where affinity maps to different quant profiles and measure degradation.
- Cold restart under pressure: simulate GPU OOM, measure graceful degradation with partial eviction and automatic model fallback policies.
- Cost model integration: build a micro-cost estimator for kernel residency vs expected token-savings from prefix-prefetch to auto-suggest cap sizes per customer.

Action items:
- (Marco) add trace spans for tile dispatch and KV migration (PR: #42) — due 2026-03-08
- (Jing) run 4x A100 multi-GPU sharded experiment, collect NVLink perf counters — due 2026-03-15
- (Evan) prototype console UI proposal for enabling prefix-prefetch with recommended thresholds — due 2026-03-05
- (Aisha) write short runbook for kernel_residency policies and add to dedicated onboarding docs — due 2026-03-01

Notes / gotchas observed during runs:
- Triton introspection APIs report a model as "ready" before all TRT kernels are fully warmed; the connector ended up routing some early requests to a half-warmed engine in one run which added ~30ms spikes. Add warm handshake check.
- Some custom-shim ops used nonstandard alignment and triggered cudnn alignment warnings; this inflated memory by ~300MB intermittently.
- Prefetching across tenants requires strict isolation: current slab code uses a shared allocation arena; switch to per-tenant slabs when resident-kernels>1 to avoid noisy neighbor eviction.

Conclusion:
The Trellis Connector pattern shows promise: moderate tiling + affinity routing + a measured prefix-prefetch policy yields consistent throughput and tail latency wins for mixed production workloads. However, naive aggressive tiling or oversized resident-kernels without tenant-aware quotas can cause worse tail behavior. Next step is to stabilize the hot-swap semantics, add trench tests across multi-GPU, and expose tenant-facing knobs with conservative defaults in Console.

Appendix: quick micro-benchmark snippet (pseudo):
